en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Yunwai:
Since the Buddha-dharma separated into Chan, there have been five schools of Chan. Currently, two are practiced throughout the four quarters:
the Linji and the Caodong. Nevertheless, among those who study Chan, the majority follow the Linji tradition, while the Caodong remains a solitary school.
The one who clearly illuminated the Four Ming Teachings was Chan Master Hongzhi; he was truly preeminent.
Consequently, students admired and took him as their teacher, and thus those who followed the Dongshan lineage were most numerous in the Four Ming region.
Now, Master Yunwai Xiu is one such figure. His virtue and wisdom shine like the sun and moon throughout the monastic community, and his disciples follow him.

Those with whom he associated were all renowned ministers and eminent scholars of the age. During his tenure at Tianning Temple, he was most intimately acquainted with my late grandfather, the Grand Tutor (Taifu Gong).
My grandfather once showed me a poem sent by the Master; at that time, I regretted not having met him.
Later, when I was assigned to teach at Xiangshan and the Master became the abbot of Zhimen, we were finally able to form a friendship beyond formal quarters. The Master...
His countenance was pure and warm, and his speech was simple and plain; he was truly what is called a man of virtue.
Subsequently, Xiao Sishi Can presented a volume of the Master’s writings and requested a preface from me. Having encountered many anxieties in the world, I have placed myself in a state of seclusion.

Whenever I am beset by mental distress and confusion, I take up these works for amusement to cleanse my worldly concerns. Thus, I have been able to examine them thoroughly; as for his poetry, it is as follows: [The poem follows]
The style of the High Tang was profound and substantial; as for its prefaces, postscripts, commentaries, and treatises, their literary brilliance was dazzling.

As for such works as gāthās, eulogies, and *nianzan* (appreciative praises), although I cannot fully comprehend their meanings, judging them by their underlying intent, none of them are mere compositions.
Alas! Virtuous conduct is the root of a person; words and speech are but its branches and leaves, and are not sufficient [to define one].

The Master has ceased [his journey]. The Master is still in the prime of his years; his Way is about to be realized, and he will surely be able to greatly revitalize the tradition of our school so that its teachings fill the world.
Is this not what this record says? The Master’s name is Yúnxiù; “Beyond the Clouds” (Yúnwài) is his title.
At this time, on the third day of the sixth month of the gengzi year in summer, Chen Sheng, a literary scribe from Mount Xiangshan, respectfully prefaces this:

With Mount Taibai as a screen and twenty li of pines as a seat, how many people have failed to recognize that the shadows of the clouds conceal their very selves? How many have let the opportunity slip away?
A missed opportunity. He was originally an ancient Buddha from Xizhou who has returned once more. One must strictly avoid explaining it before the pivot of the teaching.

But tell me, what is it like after it has been explained? A curtain of night-brightness hangs from the peak of Mount Sumeru; a rolling pearl falls through the air. (In another edition, there is the character "wai" [external] beneath "ying" [shadow].)
Eulogy on the Table of Contents of the Recorded Sayings of Master Yunwai by the Elder Huanzhu, Zhongfeng.
Bowing in homage.
Recorded Sayings, Verses on Ancient Cases (Nian-gu),
Verses on Ancient Cases (Song-gu), Ritual Ceremonies (Fo-shi),
Eulogies for Patriarchs (Zu-zan), Verses, and Prefaces and Postscripts from the Chan Temple of Zhuzhimen.
Supplement to the Recorded Sayings of Master Yunwai of Zhimen Chan Monastery,
compiled by his junior disciple, the bhikṣu Shican.
Small Sermon upon Admission to the Monastery: A grove of sandalwood is surrounded by sandalwood;
a grove of thorns is surrounded by thorns; a grove of lions is surrounded by lions; a grove of tigers and wolves is surrounded by tigers and wolves.
Within Mount Bairyam, these four kinds of groves are arrayed together in a jumble. This mountain monk has never usually made such clear distinctions; yet, having arrived here—
He could not help but snap his fingers once, intending to transform the tigers and wolves into lions and the thorns into sandalwood.

Without speaking, they transformed themselves; without being governed, they were no longer in disorder. Thus one sees a sandalwood grove where no other trees grow, dense and profound, where the lion dwells.
He planted his staff upright and said, "The lion roars!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "At midnight the golden crow emerges; its vast radiance illuminates the entire universe. Two eyes face the green mountains; my whole body weeps like rain.
At such a moment as this, Chan Master Tong of Daochang Temple in Huzhou tames tigers."

The Buddha ascended the hall after his enlightenment. On the eighth night of the twelfth lunar month, at the fourth watch of midnight, the Great Awakened World-Honored One beheld the morning star and attained the Way.
This led all his descendants of later generations to dye their hair black at midnight. Last night, Zhimen caught a cold and sneezed;
it happened to coincide perfectly.
Ascending the hall, he said: "There are four types of meaning in speaking of Chan. Sometimes the intent reaches but the words do not; it is like writing characters in empty space.
Sometimes the words reach but the intent does not; it is like a clearly defined title. Sometimes both words and intent reach; it is like having already discerned the 'bow-snake' illusion."
Sometimes both word and meaning fail to reach [the mark]; one must strictly avoid "killing" [the living truth]. If you deliberate in such a manner, you will entirely fall ill with words and meanings.

On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and offered incense, saying: "The phoenix calendar marks a new beginning; of its three hundred and sixty days, there is end and there is start."
The Golden Wheel-turning King ruled for eighty-four thousand years; the more time passed, the longer it seemed.

To ascend the hall [for formal teaching] while binding one’s feet in full lotus posture is to dream atop a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. To set one's mind upon books and scrolls is to search for a needle at the bottom of the great ocean.
When the entire body falls away, the dream is shattered and one awakens. Only when the single thought remains unmoved does one finally realize where the needle was all along.
Furthermore, tell me: what is it like after awakening? Give me back my needle!
Small Retreat *Sāman* (General Address): The *Gaṇḍavyūha* monastery is established everywhere; it perfectly encompasses the three periods of time, being neither destroyed nor mixed.
The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present have now entered its perfect clarity;
those who practice and study in the future should abide according to this. At the foot of White Rock Mountain there is an ancient temple where the Chan practitioners of the ten directions gather.
For ninety days, in accordance with the holy regulations of the Tathāgata, each shall observe the *kaṭhina* retreat and protect all living beings. Each...

Each shall establish a deadline to realize the fruit. This mountain monk and all of you shall cultivate pure conduct with one body and one life, entering the Great Treasury of Luminous Supernatural Powers.
Among them, there may be those who hold heterodox views or those who are merely vague and indistinct.
Those who are not of the same wisdom as I are banished to other worlds. Why? "The heron standing in the snow is not the same color; the bright moon among the reeds is not something else.
Citing an ancient worthy’s saying: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. The verse says: Having long thirsted, one meets sweet rain. He...
Having seen it in the past, one knows it now: on the night of the flower-lit bridal chamber, the golden-plaque valedictorian returns.

Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "The waters of Kunlun are easily released; the spring of Shaolin is difficult to make fragrant. One arm was suddenly severed, and for nine years all was forgotten.
Thunderous patterns appear upon the tusks of elephants; flowers brew honey within the hives of bees. Branches diverge and lineages split—thus do the sons..."
The details are numerous and fragmented. A crow is not a horse, yet they resemble one in speech and writing.
On the occasion of Secretary Xie’s initial ascent to the hall, [the Master said]: "To study and practice it constantly—is that not joyful?
To have friends come from afar—is that not a delight? That others do not understand you and you remain free of resentment—is that not the mark of a gentleman? Now tell me, what about the drumming?
Ascending the hall: For what reason did he read a chapter of the *Analects*? "Using a wedge to extract a wedge. Regarding the *Xiaochan* (Small Retreat) *Xican* (General Instruction):
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, though unbound, it was bound; one dwells halfway along the path. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, though bound, it was unbound;
one returns home and sits securely. These are the matters of the mountain monk’s journey during the ninety days.
The people do not know this. Within ninety days, I, this mountain monk, know all the affairs within their households.
Since I know them, whether they can realize the proof at the appointed time or not is set aside for a moment.

It is simply like when the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, on the Buddha’s Day of Joy and the day of the Monks’ Prātimokṣa, placed food and drink of a hundred flavors within an *urunda* bowl and offered it to the Buddha.
"And when the Sangha repays the kindness of their parents who raised them with such love and compassion, do they still possess the breath of a true monk?
After a long silence, he said: "When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence; when the wise see it, they call it wisdom.

He cited Master Dongshan Shoujie’s instruction to the assembly: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, go east or go west—to where there is not a single inch of grass for ten thousand miles."

The Hermit of Liuyang heard this and said, "Stepping out the door is already walking in the weeds. [Zhaozhou] picked up the case and said, "When the Hermit of Liuyang spoke thus, how many people did not dare to step out the door?"
Ascending the hall: At midnight, the great void is split asunder; at high noon, the sun shines brightly upon the day. All phenomena are concealed—a single mass of raw iron.
Both are set aside; there is yet another matter for deliberation: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of the South Sea sits upright in the Moon-on-Water Dharma-hall.
Master Xie Zunsu ascended the hall. The spring mountains layer upon layer in wild green; the spring waters ripple in empty azure.
Vast and silent between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one gaze toward? At the point where the Patriarch Mingjue arrived, the attendant knows it;
this mountain monk’s staff also knows it. [He] struck the ground with his staff and said, "The attendant knows it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Thirty years ago, at the house of Shen Shierlang beneath Mount Daochang in Huzhou, a male ox gave birth to a female calf.
I have told this to you all, yet you do not believe me. I went personally to his house to borrow it for a look."
Two horns point toward heaven; four hooves tread upon the earth; his tail fans the wind; his nostrils draw in the air.
Before his teeth have even grown, he already understands the business of plowing fields and harrowing the soil. Tell me, is this extraordinary or not? Striking the meditation seat, he said:
"No one in the world knows this meaning."

The Buddha’s Nirvana Hall. On the fifteenth day of the second month, between the twin *śāla* trees in Central India of the Western Heaven, there was one Buddha who attained extinction, named Śākyamuni.

His voice and teachings spread far and wide. Two thousand years later, beneath White Rock Mountain in the land of China in the East, there is a descendant who burns incense in longing remembrance. But tell me, what is it that he longs for?
[The Master says: "Ma! This golden body with its eighty minor marks cannot be found anywhere in heaven or on earth.
*Verse for the Abbot Hai upon ascending the hall:* The west wind withers the tree leaves; The cricket cries by the ruined wall.
The bright moon shines through the broken roof; The dew chills the golden bed. One scroll of the Tripitaka, one chapter of a Confucian text— Neither can be read to the end, nor written out.
Accomplishing Practice. "The sky is vast and the earth is wide—who can deliberate upon this?

He ascended the hall and said: "As the first light of dawn begins to part, the rooster crows; before the spring breeze has stirred, the birds sing. Upon a single bed, every household dreams of a butterfly;
as for the meaning of the Patriarchs, no one is willing to enter into contemplation."

I request the two classes of assembly to take their places in the hall. Looking left and right, all present are my worthy assistants. Clouds arise and follow the dragon; winds arise and follow the tiger.
As this mountain monk sits upon the rope seat to preach Chan, he presses his staff and acts as the host. After a long silence, he says: "Pǔ! (Universal).
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: This monastery possesses the marks of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), with boundary-stones marking its four corners:
the southeast corner, the northeast corner, the southwest corner, and the northwest corner. Once the boundary has been established by following the cord, it is called "Pure Ground" (śuddha-bhūmi).

During the three months of summer, the patch-robed monks (cīvara-dhara) dwell in retreat; anyone who transgresses the marks of the Great Boundary is a monk who has broken the precepts. Thus does Zhimen announce.
[The respondent] replied: "Perhaps there is a monk who comes forward and says, 'This is no place for studying the Vinaya;
why do you engage in such talk? To which the Chan practitioner would reply: 'We take the four great continents as the boundary markers. One may go east, one may go west.'"
"One may go south; one may go north. When the mountain monk was confronted with this question, he could do nothing but lower his head and return to the abbot’s quarters.
Why? Because he thought there was no one [capable of answering]. It is said: "In the Western Heaven (India), they used a wax man as a test; in this land (China), they use an iron ball as a test.
If one follows the laws of the Western Heaven, one violates the pure regulations of this land. If one follows the regulations of this land...
The Pure Rules (Qinggui) violate the laws and decrees of the Western Heaven; thus, Zimen could not help but establish separate regulations.
But tell me, what serves as proof? Wait until you realize the Way through the whisk.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The cricket cries by the ruined wall; the frog calls across the spring waters. It is the seasons that cause this; everywhere it clamors in people's ears.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva seeks out sounds to save beings from suffering, yet he cannot save them. Instead, he comes to ask the mountain monk:
'Is there some other principle? To which I immediately say: 'Stop! Stop!'"
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. With his whisk, he draws a circle and says, "It encompasses heaven and earth.
Holding the whisk upright, he says, "This is what Baizhang realized and what Huishan stirred. Today, Zhimen brings it forth in brilliance;
ten million loads of black firewood are emitting light and manifesting auspicious signs. All people throughout the world may freely come toward the fire."
Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: A single phrase—mysterious within the mysterious, wondrous within the wondrous. Cold and heat do not interfere; yin and yang do not reach it.
Ultimately, how does one pass through this? "The egret standing in the snow is not of the same color; the bright moon among the reeds is not like that."
Ascending the hall, Master Wansong cited the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* of the *Mahāyāna-śrī-mahā-sannipāta-sūtra*:
"At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; do not attempt to extinguish those deluded minds; do not apply cognitive discernment to the realm of deluded thoughts;

and do not, in the absence of such discernment, discriminate what is real. "Excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners! If the ice on the Hutuo River were to freeze over, would there truly be such a thing?"
It is simply that within this interval, the nature of water remains unchanged. (Note: The original text of the scripture has slight variations.

Small Precept Assembly on New Year’s Eve: A thousand crags are laden with snow; ten thousand waters have turned to ice. Tonight is the height of cold, the end of the year; tomorrow morning, the moon will be ever new.
This mountain monk’s whisk has hung for a long time in the corner of his meditation seat, untouched by even a speck of dust.
Picking it up with the hand of faith, spring returns to the great earth. Displaying a compassionate countenance upon the old Śākyamuni, he gathers his wrathful energy within the diamond eyes.
This single stroke is most wondrous and most efficacious. Now is precisely the time. How can one fully comprehend it?

Seeking it amidst the vast expanse of dust, one cannot find it; yet where there is no seeing, it is clearly manifest. [The Master] cites the koan of Beichan’s “Boiling the White Ox in the Open Field” and offers this verse:
At year’s end, the family is poor and has nothing left; The white ox is led out to be boiled for the sake of others.
In the hall, they do not ask how many monks there are; Each person is given their share of the soup.
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: Last night, this mountain monk had an extraordinary dream.

In the dream, he saw a single bowl of lamp lit at the bottom of the great eastern ocean, such that the waters of the four great oceans became brilliantly radiant, clearly illuminating every fish, dragon, shrimp, and crab with distinct clarity.
Then, Sāgara, the Dragon King of the Ocean, together with all the other dragon kings, went to the celestial palace of Śakra to petition him.
He reported these matters [to the Buddha]. Śakra-devānām-indra assembled the various devas and nāga kings to descend together into the Sahā world.
They inquired as to what causes and conditions had led to the manifestation of this auspicious omen. At that moment, the mountain monk awoke from his dream.
This morning happens to coincide with the Lantern Festival; it would be improper for me to recount this dream as an offering to you all. If you can believe it, then so be it.
Natural radiance shines brilliantly. If you do not believe this, how can you even wonder at it?
Upon ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat, I have swept away the nests of right and wrong and cut off the spreading vines of conceptual proliferation.
Today, I open my bag of provisions; there is no need to go east or west. Break the staff and stay right here. Why? Because of the blue-eyed one.
The Hu monk sat for nine years; his heart and gall were as if cast from raw iron.
Master Xie Zhao, Abbot, and Attendant Tang ascend the hall: Within the Tathāgatagarbha there is a perpetually perfect moon, as large as a chariot wheel and as cold as ice and snow.
How could the rhinoceros fan ever be separate? A raging tide pushes it forth from the sea—just so!
It was the Mid-Autumn Festival. If you call this "a white lotus floating out from the Dragon King’s palace," I would say that Yuchuanzi is talking nonsense.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said:
"Dharma’s eyes weigh eight bushels and four pecks; I have cut the tethering rope and threaded them through before you all."
Shaking up both heaven and earth—who has such power?

Xie Suweng ascends the high seat at the head of the assembly; his intent lies beyond words, and the Way resides before the pivot of action. Those who seek it by trying to match it with their thoughts will miss the mark.
Meeting him, he is too weary for pleasantries. His ancient sword lies buried long within its scabbard; his idle bow is never strung.
Do you all wish to recognize the true general? How vigorous and alert this old man is!
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall. He wore a broom as a dance costume and a withered bamboo stake as a cap; those who saw him considered it a strange occurrence.
But tell me, when the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger to heaven and one finger to earth, saying, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
How does this compare? It is but a hair's breadth different.
Xie Ou Shengyuan ascends the hall: "Flowing without returning is called emotion (*qing*); profound stillness without wavering is called nature (*xing*);
spiritual clarity without dullness is called spirit (*shen*); luminosity without confusion is called illumination (*ming*). To be deluded regarding these four is to be an ordinary person;
to awaken to these four is to be a sage. But tell me, who possesses these? It is the brush-tip on the nose of Bodhidharma."
Directly! The Master’s eyes are pitch black.
Entering the hall in Central China: Heaven and earth are as hot as a furnace; all things are being boiled in one cauldron. The patch-robed monk is not killed by the boiling;
coming forth, he claps his hands and dances. Do you all understand? If it were not for the spirit of Lu Sanlang, who else would dare to be so bold?
A loud voice:

An explanation for the summer retreat’s small *sīman* (private instruction). Suppose the three thousand great thousandfold world-system were entirely filled with autumn insects, each emitting its own sound without any mingling with the others.
Have you all heard them during these ninety days? If you have not yet heard them, then directly—
You must hear it and take it up. If you have already heard it, you must simply pass through it.
If you can pass through it, then come here and meet with this mountain monk; I shall bear witness for you. But tell me, what is it that is witnessed?

If you say there is something witnessed, then the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all the old monks in the world would not have attained Equal and Right Enlightenment.

Awakening. If one were to say there is nothing realized, then the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and the elder monks of the world would not have attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
Ultimately, how is it? At this point, you ought to know for yourself. Citing the words of the Patriarch Mingjue:
"Heaven and earth are tilted; sun, moon, and stars are all pitch black. East and west cannot be distinguished, nor can north and south."
"Where can one see such a fundamental monk? Xuedou commented: "There is no need for an announcement; how difficult would it be to see him? In the Hall:
"Those who study Chan must by all means not seek to 'awaken' to the Way. If you awaken to the Way, you will not attain liberation for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Why? One character entering an official gate; even a cart pulled by nine oxen cannot get out."
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: The ocean waters recede; the celestial winds grow cold. One Yang pierces through Kun;
the six Yin give birth to Qian. The Way of the gentleman grows daily longer; the Way of the petty person wanes daily. Last year, the Master of Zhimen held his staff upon the black earth;
this year, he holds his staff upon the black earth. Still as a mountain valley, yet moving like a clap of thunder. At times, he raises it...
Sometimes it is let go; sometimes horizontal, sometimes vertical; sometimes inverted, sometimes upright.
Now, at this time when the Way of the Sun shines with clarity, tell me: is it grasping or letting go? Is it horizontal or vertical? Is it inverted or upright?
How should one convey this message? He struck the meditation staff and said: "Twenty-four times the flowers [bloom]."

The wind of faith arrives first every year at the plum trees. Citing the words of the Patriarch Hongzhi: "Upon the newly emerging realm of floating emptiness, the three periods of time shift and pass;
within the firm and solid earth, there is a deep resonance as the single Yang begins to sprout. Abiding yet without abiding, it secretly turns the wheel of mechanism;
arising yet without arising, it wondrously transcends the affairs of shadows. The verse says: Hair grows and nails lengthen, ever as they are.

This: the tendons turn and the pulses vibrate; rest and do not inquire of others. Movement and stillness do not interfere with the affairs of waning and waxing. Let it be that beyond the gate the snow and cold abound.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall: "The World-Honored One’s two eyes were clear as he gazed at the stars in the heavens. Zhimen’s two eyes are clear as he gazes at the heavens."

The Upper Star: The eyes of the Gate of Wisdom are both blind; the eyes of the World-Honored One are both clear. The eyes of the World-Honored One are both blind; the eyes of the Gate of Wisdom are both clear.
For two thousand years they have alternated, each in their own mind feeling unease. "World-Honored One, World-Honored One, at this time today, who is the one beneath you?"
A Small Sermon on the Eve of the Year’s End. First function, then illumination: the three hundred and sixty days have been spent. First illumination, then function:
another day has been added to the new year’s calendar. Illumination and function simultaneous: the heavens share the white clouds at dawn; the waters flow with the bright moon.
Illumination and function not simultaneous: within the twelve hours, there is yet a slight discrepancy. To deliberate in such a manner—[is this not a great pity?]
These are always matters of the ordinary. If one does not deliberate in such a manner, what ultimate marvel could there be?

Amidst the sound of the firecrackers, eighty thousand kinds of inauspicious things are startled away; from within the horn of the plum blossoms, eighty thousand kinds of auspicious things are blown forth.
Everyone, tonight as you keep the New Year vigil, do not nod off. At the junction where two years meet, there is something here.
How strange! Tell me, what is so strange? Tomorrow is the New Year’s Day; Master Liao comes out to pay his respects.

[The Master] cites a monk who asked an ancient worthy, “What is it like when the year ends and the year is exhausted? The ancient worthy replied, “Old Wang of the Eastern Village burns paper money at night.
The verse says: Old Wang of the Eastern Village burns paper money at night; He ensures that the New Year will be better than the old.
Year. When all three divination slips fall favorably and one taps the teeth three times, it signifies peace and stability, a life of simple contentment.
This is the Small Sermon for the End of the Summer Retreat. The ancients established specific periods and limits; these were not established in vain.

To realize the truth by fixing a deadline is like a fish drinking water—it knows its temperature by itself. As it is said: "When the time and season arrive, the principle reveals itself naturally. Today is the end of the sacred summer retreat.
The announcement of completion has been made; since the time has arrived, why is it that this principle is not manifest? Everyone must simply awaken for themselves before they can succeed.
For the Master Zhimen to proclaim such things is also to cause others to increase their ignorance through idle matters.
Nevertheless, if a monk were suddenly to come forward and say, "Venerable Sir, you usually desire so much for everyone; why do you not speak of yourself? I would say to him:
This old monk is naturally able to examine and reproach his own faults; yet when others have faults, they simply do not know them. Tell me, where does the error lie?
"Ordinarily, the moon before the window is one and the same; only when there are plum blossoms does it become different. Case:
When Luzu saw a monk coming, he would turn his back to the wall. [The Master] comments: "Luzu’s establishment of a gate and its methods are indeed extraordinary, yet..."
Not knowing that the numinous tortoise drags its tail, one brushes away traces only for more traces to arise.
Entering the hall: amidst the deep mountains and rocky cliffs, there is a fragment of ancient intent. The spring birds play in the spring breeze;

each and every one has finished their song. A monk stepped forward and said: "Venerable Sir, the magpies cry out among the cold cypresses; the Heart-Seal is transmitted by them. How could it not be so?
It is not that the ancient meaning is fully revealed; rather, I say to you: even if it were uttered from the mouth of a phoenix, it would still not be it.
During the winter *xichan* (small-scale sermon), Yangshan’s hands were held too high; Old Hao’s cotton trousers were black as lacquer. For the descendants of later generations...
Three characters were transcribed as "wu," "an," and "ma," resulting in the word for "horse. Consequently, the seasonal rhythms became discordant and the Yin and Yang were thrown into confusion.

Even if one were to freeze or scorch him to death, Xiu the Elder would by no means allow himself to be turned by such influences. Suddenly, the official Zhang Shiyi said, "The Six-Cornered Pond froze over last night;

Great Thunder Peak is exhaling its breath this morning. How about that? [The Master] then addressed him: [Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Zen dialogue (likely from the *Wumenguan* or similar koan collections). The final phrase "ji xiang ta" implies the Master spoke directly to the official.]
"Way! What business is that of yours? Raise it up! Mingzhao’s head was a bit too stiff; let us go back to a warm place to deliberate.
He then added: "Mingzhao was far too deceptive. Once is enough; how can there be a second?"
**Niangu (Ten Cases)** Case:
One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.
The Master picked up the whisk and said: "Possessing the eyes of the World-Honored One, one recognizes the World-Honored One’s vulnerability;
by scratching the World-Honored One where it itches, all Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and the old monks of the world—who among them would not be delighted?"
A monk asked Qingyuan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Qingyuan replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling?
[The Master] comments: Those who dwell within the Golden Hall have never spoken of matters concerning nobility; yet they speak of nobility.
This concerns a matter of great importance. It is not for those within the Golden Hall.
A monk asked Master Mazu: "Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I pray that you, Master, will directly point out the meaning of the West."
The Master said, "I am weary today and cannot explain it for you. Go and ask Zhizang. The monk went and asked Zhizang.
Zhizang said, "Why did you not ask the Master? The monk replied, "The Master told me to come and ask you.
Zhizang said, "I have a headache today; I cannot explain it for you. Go and ask your elder brother Hai. The monk asked Hai, and Hai said:
When I arrived here, however, I did not understand it. The monk recounted this to the Great Master. The Master said, "The head of the hidden place is white;

the head of the sea is black. [The Commentator] says: Closing one's eyes and leaping across the Yellow River—leaping once, one has already crossed. Upon the world of Qingliang, one is free and at ease.
Headaches from overexertion are the most pressing concern for people today; whether one’s head is white or black, none but Mazu can fully comprehend this.
Once, when Baizhang was ascending the hall, there was always an old man listening to the Dharma who would disperse along with the assembly. One day he did not leave.
Baizhang asked, "Who is that standing there? The old man replied, "I am someone who, under the past Buddha Kāśyapa..."
At that time, there was once a person who had lived on this mountain. A student asked him, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
He replied to him, "One does not fall into cause and effect. Because of this, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
Now I request the Master to provide a turning word in his stead. Zhaozhou said, "One is not deluded regarding cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.
The Master held up his staff and said: "Falling not into cause and effect—how wild and reckless! This invites calamity. Not being deluded regarding cause and effect—how sticky and entangled!
One has never yet let go of them. There, he did not escape the body of a wild fox; here, he still falls into the trap of nobility. Tell me, how can one achieve total eradication?
One word from Baizhang, one slap from Huangbo—the Great Function manifests before us."
Lacking any established rules, they will say, "There was a red beard; now there is another with a red beard. They have utterly cut it off. Yunmen said:
"When light does not penetrate through, there are two kinds of illnesses. First, there is no clarity in all places, and there is something before one's face.
Second, even though one has penetrated so that all phenomena are empty, there is still a lingering sense, as if there were something there."
This light does not penetrate through to liberation. Furthermore, the Dharma-body also has two kinds of illnesses.
First, having attained the Dharma-body, one fails to forget the attachment to dharmas; one's own views still persist, and one falls into the realm of the Dharma-body.
Second, even if you manage to penetrate through, you must not let it pass unexamined. If you scrutinize it closely, what trace of breath remains? This too is an illness.

The Master held up his staff and said: "To eliminate the obstacle of phenomena (dharma-āvaraṇa) is still to have the obstacle of principle (tattva-āvaraṇa). To eliminate the obstacle of principle is still to have the obstacle of the great illness of purity.
There remains, furthermore, the obstacle of the emptiness of all dharmas. Once the obstacle of the emptiness of all dharmas is eliminated, there remains the obstacle of self-view.
Only when the obstacle of self-view is eliminated and one is free from self-view can one finally return home and sit securely."
The attendant Kuò raised this question for Dēngshān: "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Dēngshān said, "What? What?
Kuò said, "When the Emperor issues the command to point out the flying dragon horse, the lame turtle sticks its head out. Dēngshān then ceased speaking.
The next day, as they were coming out from the mountain bath, Xuankuo passed some tea to Xuefeng. Xuefeng patted Xuankuo’s back once.
Xuankuo said, "This old fellow has only just now glimpsed the truth. Xuefeng then ceased speaking.
The Master said: "Deshan’s conduct did not cross the threshold, nor did he sit where the eaves overhung; he honored his dwelling.

When Attendant Kuò tried to step forward, he could not enter—just like one playing the zither at the gate of the King of Qi. Though the zither may be skillfully played, what can be done when the King does not appreciate it?"
[The Master] cited the case of Guishan asking Yangshan, "Where have you come from? Yangshan replied, "From the fields. Guishan asked, "How many people are there in the fields?
Yangshan thrust his hoe into the ground and stood with his hands clasped behind his back. Guishan said, "There is someone on South Mountain cutting thatch."
Yangshan pulled up his hoe and walked away.

Nanyang Huizhong remarked, "How many people are there in the field? Yangshan replied, "There are many in the Southern Mountains. Pulling up the hoe and walking away represents the total application of the essence within the function;

planting the hoe and standing with hands clasped represents the total embodiment of the essence within the function. When Master and Son, Muzhou Daoming and Yangshan Huiji, met in this way, essence and function were united with the Way.
"A blade or an axe cannot open it.
Yangshan raised his finger and pointed at the snow lion, saying, "Is there anyone who can pass through this form?
Yunmen said, "At that moment, I would have pushed it over. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to push it over; he does not know how to lift it up."
He held up his staff and said: "There is the Snow Lion; its color is difficult to surpass. There is no Snow Lion; its color is difficult to surpass.
If there should be one who attains this color, you may preach the pure dharma to them."
Ji cites Yunmen’s question to Qianfeng: “Please, Master, answer this question. Qianfeng said, “Not yet, even for an old monk like me.
Yunmen said, “If that is so, then I am late. Qianfeng said, “Is that how it is? Yunmen said, “I thought there was a ‘Hou Bai,’ but there is also a ‘Hou Hei’!”
The Master held up his whisk and said: "One question about the future, one answer that has already passed. The momentum of such swift intelligence cannot be grasped.
Yunmen and Qianfeng beat a deafening drum; this surpasses the exquisite dancing and the blowing of flutes and pipes."
A monk asked Yangshan, "Does the Master know how to write characters? Yangshan replied, "I do so according to my capacity. The monk then circled to the right once and asked, "What character is this?
Yangshan drew a cross (十) on the ground. The monk circled to the left once; Yangshan changed the cross into a swastika (卍).
The monk then drew a circle and, with both hands, made the gesture of Rāhu grasping the sun and moon.
Deshan asked, "What character is this? He drew a circle with a *svastika* inside it. The monk then made the gesture of *Luzhide*.
Deshan said, "So it is, so it is. You must protect and uphold it well."

The Master [Xuedou] remarked: "Nāgārjuna manifested the lunar disc form (*candramaṇḍala*) and taught the Dharma while concealing his body; this was the beginning of the Perfect Circle (*yuanxiang*) within the Formless Samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
Later, National Teacher Huizhong transmitted it to Dayuan, and eventually reached Liang Wufeng, who composed forty cases, collectively titled by six names:
first, the Perfect Circle; second, the Ocean of Meaning; third, the Dark Mechanism; fourth, the School of the Patriarchs; fifth, Intentional Speech; and sixth, Silent Discourse. Dayuan...
Danyuan said to Yangshan, "The National Teacher’s ninety-seven circular diagrams are a detailed prophecy concerning you personally; you should keep them strictly secret.
Upon receiving them, Yangshan burned them. One day, as Danyuan was ascending the hall, Yangshan drew a circular diagram, presented it with his hand, and then stood with his hands folded.
Danyuan showed him his fists interlocked. Yangshan then performed a woman’s bow. This—
These are all the essence of the *yuanxiang* (perfect circle). Yangshan’s "ten characters" is the essence of the *swastika* (*wanzi*). It is the samādhi of the asuras.
Generally speaking, the *yuanxiang* possesses its causal origination and its intentional language; it contains the wondrous meaning of all Buddhas.
Those who do not understand this and merely draw circles to deceive people are in error. (According to the *Zongxue*, this may also be called *zixue*—the study of characters.)
Ancient Verses (Ten Cases):
When the World-Honored One was born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth, saying, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored."
The lotus leaves are round and round, as round as mirrors; the water chestnuts are sharp and sharp, as sharp as awls.
How vexing it is that these ancients lacked any wisdom—they preemptively stole a couplet from my poem!
A monk asked Caoshan, "What is it like when the spiritual robe is not yet hung? Caoshan said, "Today is the completion of the mourning period for Caoshan.
The monk asked, "What is it like after the mourning period is complete? Caoshan said, "Caoshan enjoys fine wine."
Filial piety fulfilled at Mount Cao, he cast off his commoner’s robes; in refined elegance, he yields to the son of a noble house. His father is dead, yet he has wealth to spend;
drunk on wine, he sings wildly, sporting day after day.
Linji instructed Sansheng, saying, "After my passing, you must not let the treasury of my true Dharma eye be extinguished.
Sansheng replied, "How would I dare let the Master’s treasury of the true Dharma eye be extinguished? Linji said, "If someone were to ask you, how would you answer?
Sansheng then gave a shout. Linji said, "Who would have known that my treasury of the true Dharma eye was entrusted to a blind donkey?"
It is extinguished at the edge;
the oil within the lamp has been exhausted. Having cast forth its radiance to illuminate the nine provinces, a torrential rain and violent winds blow it out;
the light is no longer at the head of the old bed.
Linji questioned Huangbo about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; three times he was struck.
With intent, he met the mark on his forehead three times; without intent, he leaped over the Dragon Gate. Returning, he pondered it in the cold stillness:
the painful spot is hard to forget—it is not for lack of kindness.
Master Yù was once observing a monk who had asked Fǎdēng, “How does one advance further from atop a hundred-foot pole? Dēng replied, “Mute.
Yù studied this for three years. One day, while crossing a bridge, he stepped on a plank that broke, and he attained awakening.
Advancing further from the top of a hundred-foot pole—clearly, one more mute word adds nothing. Who has not yet reached the top of that pole?
Even they speak of the Peng bird soaring ninety thousand li.
Yunmen said: "Awakening to the Way upon hearing sound; clarifying the mind upon seeing form. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva came with money to buy sesame cakes;
when he let go of his hand, it turned out to be steamed buns."
Packing my travel gear, I set out early; meeting an old friend, we discussed the Way. Returning home, we shared three cups of wine together;
before we knew it, the sun at the edge of heaven had grown dim.
Whenever Master Jueyi was questioned, he would simply raise a single finger.
The spring breeze of three months has opened the peony; The practitioner speaks in vain of "viewing the flowers. This is not the hand of Zhao Chang of this world;
Even with brush and ink, it would be difficult to paint.
Shushan went to Weishan and asked, "I have heard your teacher say that 'the phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree.
If suddenly the tree falls and the vine withers, where do the phrases return? Weishan laughed loudly.

A skilled physician takes the patient by the hand as soon as the illness is diagnosed; he administers a wondrous medicine whose efficacy is beyond dispute. After a single dose, the patient is allowed to succumb to confusion;
yet after three days or five, they naturally regain their spirit.
Master Mazu was unwell. The head of the monastery asked him, "How is your health these days, O Monk?
The Master replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face.
He answered the sincere inquiry with sincerity; there was not a single word that was false. Alas, it is a pity that [the questioner] lost the opportunity at that moment.
Intention! Even until now, the words have not yet reached their full completion.
Aṅgulimāla saves a woman from the perils of childbirth;
a sage ruler transmits his commands. The *kegu* drum is repeatedly beaten to urge the blossoms to open—a single air of springtime radiance before one’s eyes.
Excellent. On a warm day, the oriole’s song comes forth from the valley.

Chao Wei-na Raising the Coffin (Wind Illness).

He reviled the Third Patriarch to repent of his sins and seek medical aid; he laughed at Kebin for eating the staff and leaving the monastery. Not falling into either of these two paths, he completely transcends the view of death.
A five-colored auspicious qilin strides across the celestial shore.
The bones of the monk Yuandu lie deep in the abyss;
they are white as snow. Consciousness in the skull is exhausted; the eyes are devoid of blood. A three-legged donkey prances on its hooves;
turning its body, it tramples the moon upon the clear pool.

At Ningdu Temple, the four great elements of this illusory body were ablaze amidst the shifting sands and waters of birth and death. When the wind stilled and the waves subsided, the sun rose over the western horizon.
Striking a circle with his staff, he said: "If you can recognize the formless body here, the youth of the fire-element dances within the flames."

Yandu Si entered the very marrow to serve his teacher’s stupa, employing the Great Array (Dà-yǎn) to clearly penetrate birth and death. In the midst of the bustling marketplace, he cast off the root-dusts; the leaking oil lamp was never originally his own self.
Even when a fierce fire burns it to ashes, there still remains this "little bit. But tell me, what should be done with this little bit?
How shall it be settled? The spring breeze of the third month; a single cry of the cuckoo. Again, wondrously returning to the path: the child goes back to the father.
The clouds gather, and the green mountains open the doors of the stupa.
O noble one, though the eyes,
ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all simultaneously lost, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena remain as they were.
Look for yourself within this mass of blazing flames.
The fire of the seat-priest penetrates everywhere;
it is his entire body, it is his whole being. When the pure water pitcher was kicked over, he recognized that which has been with him all along. Throwing out the fire, he said:
"How could this fierce fire ever burn the dead?"
Shi Jingtou threw fire-sticks into the fire to make a sound; he struck stones to produce fire. He cleared away all his worldly possessions until not even a single thread remained upon him.
Having endured until he reached the platform of nirvana, it was still just this very thing—this very thing which he tabooed by calling it "fire."
The very center of the fire at the head quarters of the monastery is just this. Birth-and-death and nirvana are just this.
What is this? A stone window and a lamp; it cannot be destroyed by fire.
Before his passing, Layman Huàn’ān frequently met me;
after death, we have encountered once more. On the northern and southern banks, the duckweed flowers face the red *liǎo* plants.
(Name of person): Because the illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease; because the illusory objects cease...
Therefore, when illusion ceases, it also ceases; because the cessation of illusion has itself ceased, that which is not illusion does not cease.

Reaching this point, one seals the many-mouthed chatter of Old Pang and shatters the single silence of Vimalakīrti. Tell me, right now, as you enter the great mass of fire, perform the great Buddha-work!
Furthermore, how is it? The fire-dragon pearl flies forth from the skull; at the tip of the coral tree, the sun shines bright.
Master Han holds the torch as the wind scatters golden leaves across the gate. A long, winding ancient road leads out from the desolate village. I urge you: go straight ahead and do not turn back.
We bow our heads; returning to the West before the sun has set. (Name of person). As husband and wife, we are bound by karmic conditions;
life after life, birth after birth, we are nothing but kin. We share in life together and die together; in life and death we shall not be parted.
From beginning to end, we shall be companions on the Way. Among our neighbors and clansmen, we shall be praised for our benevolence; among our own kin, we shall be praised for our righteousness.
To teach one's sons and instruct one's grandsons so that they may read the *Shijing* and understand propriety;

at eighty-three years of age, to recite this sutra—not merely one or two scrolls while chanting for one’s own Buddha—but rather thousands and tens of thousands of times as a bridge for the final moment and a source of merit for future lives:
this is certainly praiseworthy. Yet, consider the torch-bearer of the Zhimen Gate at Guocun Hermitage; today, he acts for...
The Buddhas of the three periods of time preach the Dharma; the Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen. But tell me, what do they hear? What do they speak?
In Zhengshi Township of Xiangshan County, there was a man of the Han family and his wife, Lady Ni, who were cremated on the same day.
Within the flames, a precious lotus throne appeared, and they ascended into the void. Do you all see it? Look up!
Eight *ke* late at night; already past the shifting sands.
The Patriarch’s Praise (Ten Cases):
The Great Master, the Holy Descendant of Bodhidharma.
He shattered the heterodox views of the Great Vehicle and opened the single flower of the five petals. He established the one principle of the Empty Beam King and sat at Shaolin for nine years.
Had it not been for the divine light that aided him within the deep snows, the flame after the lamp would have nearly been extinguished and its transmission lost.
The Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Dajian, propagated and upheld the Great Dharma;
throughout the generations, there have never been a lack of worthy ones. When the flower blooms, the world arises; when the fruit ripens, Bodhi is perfected.

Having received the robe and alms bowl from the West, the lineage has been transmitted through thirty-three patriarchs. How could it be that no such person exists after the sixth? This must surely be what was spoken in the prophetic verses.

The Master of True Enlightenment of Yongjia possessed a mind like brocade, like flowers blooming in the springtime gardens of the imperial court; his extraordinary, true mechanism was like the moon shining brightly over the autumn waters and the vast sky.
He surpassed Buddhas and patriarchs and brought transformation and enlightenment to humans and devas. Having arrived at Caoxi for a single night’s stay, he returned and circumambulated...
He circumambulated the meditation seat three times and stood there. Thus, he brought to a clear end the rapidity of birth and death and severed the entanglements of right and wrong.
The Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment) Pagoda serves as a testament for future generations, and the Yongjia Collection circulates widely throughout the world.
Chan Master Zhaozhou Zhenji’s commands were like the signal flags in an army; his preaching of the Dharma was like the clouds and rain of the four seasons.

Those who heard his teaching were like the earth containing all seeds, which sprout when they receive its moisture. Even after a hundred generations, one may awaken to what he called the "dog" koan. Court.
The preceding dialogue at the East Hall and West Hall is like the Great Compassion Dharani; it can cause cliffs to split and waters to surge.
One who does not know it cannot possibly understand it.
—Linji Huizhao Chan Master.
A full shout or a half-shout is like the thunder of a drought-stricken sky; those who hear it cover their ears and flee in alarm.

Yet, when the clouds roll and the rain falls, it is able to drench and nourish the parched and withered. Although this makes it difficult for those who come to find a foothold and hard for them to settle within, [it nonetheless brings about transformation].
When one attains such a person, they will be of like kind with oneself; the Dharma and the Way will shine forth, and descendants will flourish—this is the magnificence of the foundation.

Chan Master Dahui Pujue was at times as vast as the clear sky, where the brilliant sun shines everywhere; at other times, heaven and earth were dark and gloomy, with lightning flashing and thunder rolling.
Sometimes the clouds gather up from the vast fields and the moon is reflected in the long river; sometimes the spring rain nourishes the withered, and ten thousand species of flowers bloom;
sometimes flocks of birds soar and cry as the hundred hibernating creatures open their burrows; and sometimes the north wind sweeps across the earth and the great floods surge with waves.
At times, snow fills the myriad peaks and the trees of the thousand forests break under its weight; at times, snakes and tigers block the path while fish and dragons roam the gullies.
At times, cities and districts are divided, bustling with the clamor of carriages and horses; at times, the land is vast and sparsely populated, and heaven and earth are desolate and expansive.

Indeed, though one were to exhaust the sounds and echoes of heaven and earth, one could not fathom his words; though one were to exhaust all things and phenomena within heaven and earth, one could not exhaust his utility.
Consequently, although his transgressions filled the heavens, he was exiled to Hengyang and Mei Yang for seventeen years.
Yet, neither cold nor hunger could kill him; he returned as before to the summit of Lingxiao Peak and ascended the lion throne, where he gathered one thousand seven hundred monks.
The Master surrounded by his disciples expounded the Dharma. This is what is called "Great Wisdom.
Although Zen Master Enzen of Chiku-gawa’s reputation did not rank above those of other quarters, nor did his position rank above those of other quarters, his Way stood above that of all quarters.
Shang may truly be called one who, having attained enlightenment, met a person from whom he received a formal lineage transmission. He gave this instruction:
"Everywhere else, people pull out nails, extract wedges, untie adhesions, and remove bonds for others.

Here, I add more nails, insert more wedges, apply more ropes, and impose more bonds for others, sending them into a deep pit to wait for them to realize it themselves. Today, who among those everywhere else has such words?"
Chan Master Xuedou Mingjue’s disposition was serene and detached.
The seventy-two peaks rise steeply and azure; his eloquence flows like surging waves. The three-thousand-acre lake is vast and boundless;
his literary compositions are like a forest of pearls and a mirror of brocade. As each petal of flower blooms in the warmth of spring, he illuminates the nature.
The earth is like Mount Sumeru amidst flying snow; leaves fall one by one as autumn draws to its close. When one’s words fill the world, there is no fault in their speech;

when one’s conduct fills the world, there is no resentment or malice. With a straight hook, he fishes for the black dragon; why should he harbor any concern for shrimp, fish, crabs, or horseshoe crabs?

Having transmitted the Way, he attained the celestial robe (*t'ian yi*); his lofty essence was peerless throughout three generations. His fame encompasses heaven and earth, truly a gathering of the sublime.
When Chan Master Yunju Xiaoshun was begging for alms in Wuchang, he encountered Layman Liu.
The Layman questioned him regarding the "Ancient Mirror" koan; when their exchange reached a stalemate, the Layman gestured for him to leave.
He returned to Dongshan and repeated his previous question. Dongshan said, "It is not far from here to Hanyang. He added, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower is Parrot Isle.
Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. Only then did he realize that the ancient mirror does not depend on whether it is polished or not;

it reflects both the present and the past without error. From this time forth, his teachings never fell into conventional patterns. It was as if, when the weather was cold, one were to wash one's feet with hot water at night.
One might take off one's socks and fall asleep; at dawn, one quickly ties on one's travel-bag. If the wind blows the fence down, one calls for laborers to split bamboo and bind it back up.
How could such things possibly arise from learning and knowledge?

Chan Master Hongzhi Zhengjue of Tiantong—the ancient Buddha of Xizhou—emanated a great radiance that pervaded all places. To discuss his Way, even the Primordial Giant opening the foundation of the Great Ultimate (Taiji) would be insufficient as a metaphor;
to describe his virtue, even the Great Equilibrium (Dajun) shaping all formed things would be insufficient as a metaphor.
The moon shining over the autumn waters is insufficient to illustrate its brilliance. The clouds dispersing their colors across a clear sky are insufficient to illustrate its patterns.
The wind blowing through the clouds of the nine realms is insufficient to illustrate its movement. The earth of Mount Sumeru piled into mountains is insufficient to illustrate its stillness.
Bees in their hives brewing honey from a hundred flowers is insufficient to illustrate its subtlety.

The silken thread of an ant piercing a nine-curved pearl is not enough to illustrate its ingenuity; the sound of stringed and wind instruments played in a painted hall is not enough to illustrate its resonance;
the spring breeze entering the Garden of Jin-gu is not enough to illustrate its color.
The Son of Heaven ascending upon a phoenix and shaded by celestial fungi is not enough to illustrate his nobility;
scattering pearls within a purple silk canopy is not enough to illustrate his wealth. Alas! I shall never again behold the ancients.
Will those who compile genealogies for their descendants feel no sense of shame?
Verses (93 stanzas). Reading the Recorded Sayings of the Master:
A blue banner slants out from the painted bridge to the west; Willow flowers fly as the waters fill the embankment. One draught may lead one astray for a thousand days.
Wine: Drunk, one is buried in a desolate tomb, no thought of returning.
To Chen Taifu:
Planting bamboo and sowing flowers around the eaves of the house; Associating with monks, one also learns to wear the *pianshan* robe. In times of peace, one has seen those who cultivate the arts.
One day, the Son of Heaven searched extensively until he reached Mount Fu Yan.

Sitting alone in a room at night in the western hermitage, the cold lamp makes the night seem long. Eight thousand li of road brought him to Mei Yang; the Western Mountains are truly not as expansive as this.
Island. It is also said: "The pavilions and halls are cool with the fragrant breeze.
The ancient moon, known as the soul of the thousand-year cassia tree, refuses to die; night after night it flies above the heads of men. I always love this single square of the central courtyard.
I submit this: when ten thousand miles of vast sky are submerged in clouds, the characters in the scroll of Venerable Ziryan’s verses were not obtained easily;
once the lamp-flower fell, the five-watch bell rang, and the sound of the pitcher echoed across the broad waves of East Lake.
Far away flows a stream where frosty leaves rustle in the wind.
Master Qing (who once burned off six fingers and attained realization upon hearing the cry of the cuckoo) dwells in such a place that few practitioners can reach it.
Though he sought his six fingers again after the fire, his lingering regrets have not faded in a hundred years.
Attained. A single cry of the cuckoo stirs the heart.

On an autumn day walking through the mountains, the setting sun bathes half the valley in crimson leaves; a village of wild folk where fowl and dogs roam, and cowherd boys sing and laugh among the cattle and sheep.
Below. The pure customs of ancient times have all passed to others.
He asks about the old city’s river in the kingdom of Gandhāra; he recalls from afar the jujube tree blossoms by the riverbank. How many years have passed since the white elephant was tied there?
Far away. How can today’s affairs of prosperity and decay compare?

On the summit of Mount Jinshan, within a half-cave of rock, lies the place where the dhūta practitioner sat in meditation. His merit, once established, is as unyielding as stone; the white python has transformed into a dragon and returned to the sea.
Depart! Only an old *dhūta* remains in the mountains.
On that day at Heilin Monastery, Jia Shan met Chuanzi; even the flawless Fayan has his flaws. With a single stroke of the oar upon Zhujing, the wind and waves arise.
Urgent! Harmony shifts the roots and removes the cuckoo flowers, presenting to Master Xuewu of Zhongzhu the layered *Avataṃsaka* realm of the Dharma-world:
smoke and willows fill the city as spring deepens; with a snap of the fingers, the gate opens and we meet.
Later, when Sudhana’s worldly mind was extinguished like ashes, he sought his friend’s mountain hermitage;
as his journey through the fine peaks reached its end, his eyes opened once more. Vegetable leaves and golden coins drifted with the water—do not say that the gate of leisure is easily found.
Covered. Beside the pines there is a path where no moss grows.

The snails have borrowed the feet of the mulberry worms; their offspring’s cries resemble my own as I offer prayers morning and evening. It is precisely because they have prayed so thoroughly that they are thus.
It seems that for generations they have been unable to raise their gates high.
The life of a honeybee need not fear taxes; in a single day, how many times does it pass through the gardens? Its thighs grow weary, yet it never tires of the flower pollen.
Heavy. Year after year, one only loves the abundance of one's descendants.
Behold Mingjue’s words:
"A waterfall of over a thousand fathoms of white snow; seventy-two peaks of Dongting Lake in the cold. Had he gathered it back at that time—
[Colophon]. Who would have known that this record was a separate transmission?
Master Taoyuan (Tangyan) presented this to Master Yingzong.

Formerly, we had formed a bond of friendship for three years while he resided in seclusion at Seng'an; once he settled in Xiacheng, we had not expected to meet again. Now that I hear he has already departed for Tianzhu, [I am filled with grief].
The temple; hearing the news of its demise, the white-haired master’s heart breaks.
After the fire at T’ien-ning, the kalpa-fire blazed so fiercely that everything was utterly destroyed. To follow him or not to follow him—the spring wind blows across the scars of the burn.
Green. The pavilions and towers remain as they were, yet many are there.

Lamenting for my attendant Xinglin, amidst three calls of his name, he bore an injustice. He would have raised a hundred thousand troops to defend the city; who knew that before Mount Handan, [the truth lay hidden]?
On the road, he carved his name into a tree where ambushes lay in wait.
He visited the pagoda of Master Zizide of Jingci Temple.

He produced the "Six Oxen Diagram" at Xinfeng Qu. His wondrous songs were difficult to harmonize with, yet their transmission became increasingly corrupted. The life-essence of the Dharma hangs by a single thread; the gates of the school are in peril.
Heavy. Unbidden, tears fall upon the courtyard *śāla* grass.

Upon the wondrous high terrace, reaching toward the heavens, the sky gradually lowers. Taking another step upward, with whom shall one return? Within the breast, one must resolve the affairs of a lifetime.
The matter: A solitary crane flies among the branches of a pine tree.
Reading the words of the late Master Gujian, I see the head librarian Isō returning to Changzhou:
"At the tip of the golden needle, the mandarin ducks take flight; within the path of the jade thread, the egrets soar. Far away, the three ten-thousand-li of Lake Dongting."
Recently, the spring waves have been boundlessly green and rippling.
I observe Master Hei-an’s painting of the bridge;

upon this bridge, one may achieve fame and office for fifty years. Yet those who greedily rush forward—who would be willing to look back at the perilous fall? In this world, many speak of practicing benevolence.
In principle, you resemble my late teacher in that your conduct is complete.

When I met an old farmer, a white-haired elder, I asked: "In which village do you dwell? Across the stream are smoke-shrouded trees and a bamboo-fenced gate. This year you are eighty; truly, you have nothing [to worry about]."
With all my strength, I laboriously lead the ox to replace my grandson.

Mourning for my kitten, who perished like a flower, it was as if a son had been lost. For three years, it accompanied me through my solitude. Now there is a coffin, and it is buried in the green mountains.
Your feet are still lacking the merit of the *kīla*-stone pillar.
You, Master Dongzhou, dwell in the West Ravine Hermitage within the city of purple roads and red dust;
amidst clear springs, white rocks, and drifting clouds, your gate remains as undisturbed as ever.
Silence. Flowers and birds do not come; the mind and its objects are empty.
Two Poems on Mooring at Cao'e Creek:
The ancient stele of "Yellow Silk" is a matter of a thousand years; Marsh flowers and bank grasses by the old riverside village. Night after night, I see the bright [moon] in the heart of the waves.
Moon. I suspect this is the soul of Cao E fallen into the water;
the boat halts upon the river as the tide has not yet turned. The events of the Han’an era enter my thoughts once more. On the wild bridge, I recognize the path to the village ahead.
I have read the inscription in the temple of Cao E.
Secretary He Qi: From his brush emerge the styles of Zhong and Wang;

he is a calligraphic sage in the manner of Cao. Within his breast, the poetry of Jiao and Dao abounds like the rich compositions of the Tang. Since the departure of the Buddha of the Bamboo Grove, there has been no "Buddha of Literature";
today we joyfully encounter a "Monk of the Hanlin."

Master Huì'ēn, Director of the Repository, has visited because you have constantly remembered Yunmen Temple. Over the past five or six years, we have met twice. My poetic lines grow old along with my autumning hair;
this traveler’s body is as leisurely as drifting white clouds.
In mourning for the friend Master Uisan of Donggao, who built Donggao Temple with empty fists;
he fed many monastics from the four quarters until their bellies were full. Though a hundred years have passed since his death, he has not diminished in the least;
his prayer beads and teeth continue to radiate brilliant light.

In Master Jue’an’s room, he asked, "What kind of matter is being clarified by raising one's feet? The monk replied, "It clarifies the matter of the single color. The Master held up a bamboo stick and asked, "What is this?
The monk replied, "A bamboo stick. The Master seized him and gave him a severe beating. Reflecting on this past event, [the monk] composed this verse:

In the inner chamber, he once suffered the painful blow of a bamboo staff; had he let it pass casually, he would have fallen into delusion.
Reflecting on the matter of clarity within the single color, one must skillfully gather the words that can answer the Master.
The Venerable Xuzhou of Lingyin had once served as the summer retreat master for three consecutive years.
During his time in the meditation hall, he constantly raised the phrase, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing," without changing it for three years.

At that time, it was like looking at the moon through a thin silk gauze; one did not dare utter a word. Later, when he moved his quarters to Jingci Temple, he continued to bring up this phrase. Suddenly—
Chaozhou said of himself: "To speak in such a manner is to fall into the three evil realms.
Alas, I shall not see that old monk again. Now, I have composed this verse to record it:
It is neither mind nor an object; it is Buddha. The words he bestowed within the hall were most clear. Indeed, after three years, there was one who set his heart upon them.
Regarding this matter: beneath the stupa, the golden bones remain spiritually efficacious.
