Go! Those who do not understand say that I actually answered this question; yet they fail to realize it was but a dream-talk.
At the time, I did not reveal the truth. Now I shall compose a verse:
The startling lines obtained in a dream may seem suspicious; Yet they were perfectly suited for replying within the room. Nanquan’s oil-cakes on the farm—
Offerings. Even while eating, it still relieves the hunger in the belly.
I pay distant homage at the stupa of the Old Monk of Mount Wu-shan;
my clumsy mouth has no words, yet my heart knows itself. Facing others, I shed tears that soak my dhyāna robe. Now I wish to speak of those times.
The Matter: The stupa was at Mount Wu, yet he did not see the Master.
He thanked the Venerable Tiantong for visiting;

the arrival of the elder’s carriage at the thatched cottage brought honor, and both young and old were all struck with wonder. Before he had even finished offering a single incense stick, he took his leave.
Bowing. Twenty *li* away, pine-clad clouds enter my dreams in their azure hue.
Sent to the Reverend Daboguo Du'an, who dwells among those of the Phoenix Mountains:
when we meet in dreams, it is as if in person. Old age has not yet exhausted the affairs of this world.
In the thirty-ninth year, I was left alone with my own body.
I mourn that the ancient monk Qizhen has departed;
the high branches of the willow are broken and the phoenix has flown away. The mountain colors coalesce in sorrow like extinguished embers, as the winds and rains of late spring stir my lamentation.
Darkness. Amidst the clamor of a hundred birds and the fragrance of blossoms, I see off a traveler journeying to Qiantang.
A single lake of spring water at Yongming Temple, and a hundred thousand households at Fengle Lou—take up your staff for this brief excursion; do not weary yourself.
Folded. In old records, it was said that my mountain hermitage was in Mingzhou. When Master Dumu sat waiting for the world to attain peace, it was originally I who did so;
yet when he buried his troops to challenge me, you emerged victorious. Beneath the iron *tufutu* tower, we once faced one another.
Behold! The lamp-flower blooms through five nights of spring.
Thank you, Magistrate Gao;

from house to house and family to family, hands are raised in prostration. Throughout the entire district and its three sub-prefectures, there is no injustice; the breadth of your heart across the hundred-li reaches like the autumn waters.
Purity. Wind gives rise to waves; the moon produces light.

Once again I traveled to the temple in Wu, crossing south to the Sanzhong Temple of the Wu family. The old monks have all died, yet the trees are planted anew. Walking along the corridors, I inquire of Non-characteristic (Wuxiang).
Consciousness. To recognize the profound truth is to return to one’s original abode.

Sending the Venerable Wiling to travel to Tiantai—to seek the tracks of the ox along the road to Tiantai. Waterfalls a thousand fathoms deep fly with the moon; it is said that at Stone Bridge one cannot walk.
It is attained. Year after year, spring rains grow upon the mossy robes.
One should observe that the sun and moon travel from east to west without ceasing; when meeting, there is no need to ask "how. The pines among the mountains must surely provide food for people.
Few indeed; in this world, dreams of gold are most numerous.

Entrusting myself to the Venerable Xushì, we dwell together as a single cloud over the Western Mountains. Morning and evening, the sounds of bells and chimes are heard from one another. At that time, [I was between] Tiantai and Nanyue.
As for these matters, the various sentiments within cannot yet be discussed.
Having resided with Master Dongsheng at the Yewang Monastery for over thirty years, I have had no old friends;
I remain alone amidst the clouds, my idle body accompanied only by the vast sky. Last night, I entered the Imperial Calligraphy Hall in a dream.
The gate opens; the doors and windows open wide to reveal the sun’s orb.
Entrusting this to Zen Master Guangen Zangshan:
the Buddha-dharma of years past remains unasked of. Golden leaves piled high do not change one’s official rank. A single scroll of mountain-dwelling poetry—more.
Very well. Regarding the incense burning, it may simply be viewed as part of the scripture.
Two Poems on Painting Lotus Flowers:
Three thousand beautiful maidens learn the courtly makeup; They monopolize the fragrant waters of one quarter. I ask the painter: where did you find such inspiration?
It has moved here; for five months now, the Mirror Lake has been cool.
Tens of thousands of green blades are held aloft in jagged array. A single loom of brocade is spread across like a bolt of silk. Joyfully facing the warm breeze, it is captured in this description;
the autumn winds and night rains dare not know.
A Summer Night;
Pursuing the Cool Moon, the courtyard is filled with light. Upon the pond of the Xie family, the old mountains remain green. I am ashamed to have nothing worthy of this companionship;
I simply take my Zen mind to accompany the moon’s clarity.
Borrowing the intent [of the original], I thank the descendants of the Wang family, for whom there are many; the elegant figures of Jin’s mountains and rivers remain.
Though heaven has crumbled and earth grown old, today this true copy of the *Lanting Ji* remains undiminished.

Hearing the cuckoo, the mountain moon is newly bright; the grasses and trees are cool. Overcome by traveler’s longing, I lodge in a cave-dwelling. The spring breeze refuses to cease its blowing year after year;
the resentment of the cuckoo for its lost home is likewise long.

Clearly realizing that the myriad phenomena do not invade the single thought of emptiness, Throughout the lands as numerous as dust motes, no trace remains. The spring breeze comes and picks up the willow flowers;
When concentration arises, it is the bell of the ancient temple on the western mountain.
Seeing off Chen, the School Registrar, as he seeks an official post:
"How could you know that the monk is even colder? With sincere farewells, he ascends the western dais;
the golden flower is but a red silk fan—once he has attained fame and fortune, it shall come sweeping across the earth."

In the same rhyme as Master Wantang’s “The Ten Thousand Valleys Are Silent, the Moon Fills the Mountains”: It is easy to look upon, yet difficult to enter. In years past, there was Hongtang Fort in Min;
How can it compare to this single pass amidst the clouds?
Two Poems on Dreaming Rabbit horns emerge towering from an elephant’s head; In the six streets, phoenix balls are struck in unison. A crow plunges into a black marsh as clouds gather;
A heron rests by the silver river as the moon shines in autumn.
The ancient family style is thoroughly pure and bright; at the hall of the bright moon, the night is at its height.
Regarding the secret matters of the forty-one bridges, within the range of vision, they are passed through as a single bridge.

The autumn oriole calls amidst crimson leaves like blossoms, as the morning sun dries the dew. Deep within the forest, the yellow oriole cries out; its sound is just like the whispering of spring breezes.
Yet it sings toward the west wind—a time that is no longer right.
Watching the Moon on an Autumn Night:

The falling leaves and empty mountains are most abundant in autumn. Ascending the tower, one can do nothing but marvel at the moon’s brilliance. This old monk finds his poetic lines increasingly refined;
The night snow swells the stream like the blossoms of buckwheat.

Residing at the Deer Park, my elder brother Master Zhongzhang has grown old here with the gait of a crane and the form of a tortoise; whenever I think of you, you are ever present in my heart. When shall we meet again by the green lamp at night upon our mats, to converse together?
Our hearts' desires for a hundred years have been thwarted.
To the Abbot Tan of Xiangtian:
Gazing far westward, the Yue mountains are green; how many stages of water-dwelling and mountain-treading have there been?
Out of remembrance for the traces left by the ox-plowing, though the labor of mind is bitter, the body remains unwearying.
Entrusting this to the elder brothers at Wansong on Mount Xiangshan:

the noble family’s gate flourishes with the fragrance of the cinnamom trees. In our comings and goings, we have often had the opportunity to discuss the subtleties of the Dharma. Yet, another three years have passed since we last saw one another;
gazing toward White Rock Mountain, the mountain vapors darken the air.
I address Senior Seat Gu-lin Daibai:
"The green mountains always lift their feet; after the former master passed away, Chang-geng appeared. It was not that Sudhana manifested himself at every door;
he simply wanted the Buddha-dharma to flourish in the South."
The Dharma-relative Zhezang finished his talk on hardships and perils as night drew on; the lamp-flower opened and fell two or three times. Brothers, there is no need to meet frequently;
the hair turns gray from worry all too easily.
To Master Zhou of Dongchan Temple:
The four seas and the six classes of people all rush after profit; you, Master of Dongchan, speak only of Chan. In what year did you go to dwell at Ling Shan Temple?
You invited me to the mountain crags to watch the white monkeys.
Inscribed on the Small Pond of the Purple Stone Chan Room:
Ten feet of earth were excavated before the window; A hundred-peck spring secretly connects to the ocean floor. Willow catkins transform into duckweed and do not float away;
Before one’s eyes, one wins a patch of clear blue sky.

Entrusting my studies to my elder brother, Master Tongyuan, I return to the pine and chrysanthemums where the fragrance fills the old fence. To live in a house borrowed from another is not as good as returning home. Is it that there is no strategy within your breast?
You fold your hands by the chessboard and watch the game unfold.
A Letter Sent to Chen Zhang, Also Addressed to Master Langpeng, at the Daoist Abode beside Mr.
Fu’s Residence: Within the Jasper Clouds on Mount Linggui, One refines elixirs and shall surely ascend as an immortal.
They must surely laugh that our scholar’s cap has long been a source of error.
Entering the gate at Lanwu Monastery, one immediately perceives the spirit of the Xiang River; counting the grains of its subtle fragrance, one beholds Qu Yuan.
If the mugwort and wormwood were made to share the same color, the pure character of the orchid would not be seen within the assembly.

Inscription on the Traveling Scroll of Attendant Xuan Once he carried an iron net into the vast blue sea, And returned with a single coral tree wrapped within. Lightly borrowed for a moment by the Yingdou Lake,
Its full radiance now illuminates my humble cottage.
A Letter to the Chief Librarian Renri on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:

Silver hooks and iron strokes—such calligraphy as this exists within your breast. You have gained much renown because of your writing of secular texts; how could it compare to turning your mind back toward the Inner Canon?
Devote your efforts to the volumes of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Answer: The new poem sent to me by the Abbot Taibai is rich and refined.
The pine waves for twenty li rustle and sigh. Having grown old, I am naturally aware that my tongue is short;
whenever I encounter such long compositions, I dare not offer a response.
Answer: Cease attending upon others;
why must it depend on another? There is no need for transmission. One simply seeks to pass the years without affairs. Who knows that on a single pillow, dreams are hard to achieve?
As the sun sets over the spring mountains, the cuckoo calls from every tree.
I address the Dharma friend Wuxiang of Yanshou on Mount Xiangshan, a spiritual teacher within Ruiyun Mountain:
The Way lies in traveling upon the eastern seas; turning the drum and steering the ship is a matter of ease.
When the autumn wind blows in the eighth month, the great tide rises.
To Master Doushan of Xiàngtián:
Longweng preserved the spiritual sprout in a distinct way; It was not like calling rice "rice. The winter snow joyfully presents its threefold whiteness;
The omen of a bountiful year abounds in Xiàngtián. (Those who confuse "rice" with "rice" are mistaken.)
To Master Shixin of Zhimen:
I planted bitter gourds, and bitter they were from root to tip; You planted sweet melons, yet their bitterness is even greater. This is simply due to the distinct climate and soil by the sea;
It is not because the seeds themselves have become corrupted.
The Xu family resided on the southern coast of Changguo, at the site where Master Anqi had refined his elixir.
The local tradition says that when Anqi was ten years old, his father brought him to the family mountain and instructed him, saying, "When I die, you must bury me here.
When the tide flows southward toward this place, it will provide shade for you."

On the day his father died, he followed his father’s final testament and buried him. After the family estate fell into ruin, Xu moved into the monastic life to become a śramaṇa under the Buddha’s teachings.
He has suffered many illnesses and hardships, yet fortunately has not met with death; he is now sixty-two years old.

Although I have studied the Buddha’s teachings, I possess no great wisdom; yet, having a basic understanding of the causes and effects of good and evil, I do not fall among the ranks of the ignorant and foolish.
This is truly the extent of my father’s final instructions. Now, I compose this verse to serve as a substitute for a tombstone:

The Father’s Grave within the Thousand-Household Mountains— Gazing afar, I imagine the years have long passed, And the vegetation has grown dark and overgrown. Beyond the mountains, the tide recedes, and the southern waters flow.
[The Inscription] His legacy endures for a thousand ages, reaching down to his children and grandchildren.
Weeping for Mr. Changhua Mei, Father Zhang, the Bachelor of Letters:

How could one ever repay the virtue of your father, which is as vast as heaven? Half a lifetime of drifting dreams has fallen upon your head, O Marquis. A single life remains, yet you have not yet fulfilled your wish to return home.
Zhi: Upon hearing the news of the passing, one may restrain the twin streams of tears.

At Zhūsuo, where the teachings of the Lord of the Prefecture reside, how could there be anything deemed "insignificant"? Its purity, emptiness, and cool serenity are most profound and secluded. The spring breeze returns at the tip of the whip.
It is finished. Sooner or later, the dragon’s offspring shall emerge once more.
Sent to Master Nishiya—Master Nishiya is an old acquaintance.
We have gathered for six years without parting, idly pursuing [the Way] at the roots of pines and upon the rocks.
I recall: Among the gentlemen of today, who else is there?
He sends his greetings to Master Jie of Changle:
"Neither delighting in nor dwelling in it, yet dwelling therein brings joy; how is the intent of one who delights in that joy? It is the ancestral field and its boundaries.
Vast! A single glance captures much of the autumn wind.
Sent to Master Wumen of Baoning:
Amidst the spring colors of peach blossoms on a brocade screen, within the moonlight of a snow-covered white-robed hut—at this time, with this intent, there is no one [to share it].
Meeting at the First Peak of the Immortal Mountain upon the Sea.
Inscribed on the scroll of Dharma Master Wen:
At the side of Linglong Rock, gazing at the clouds; Just as one walks beneath the moon atop Qiaozhai Peak. A single phrase: "The cypress tree in the courtyard."
My son, when have you ever composed a five-character poem?
Sent to Master Zhìpíng of Chānghuà:
"In my old age, I long remember Tángchāng Temple; shaving my hair and dyeing my robes, my resolve remains unpolished. Ten thousand layers of mountains high, two mountain streams flow."
Urgent! Upon Zhongxuan Tower, the moonlight is abundant.

The hundred-tongued bird (mynah) usually flies about seeking out other flocks; as soon as the spring breeze arrives, it sings with a hundred warbles. Its plumage is not fine, yet its tongue is slanderous.
It is well. On the peach blossom branches, one scolds the yellow oriole.
A letter sent to Master Jiang of Beishan:
do not inquire after me, for we shall not part. Pointing to my tracks, I yearn for my return; who can save me from this delay? By the Yingdou Lake, at the official post station.
Traveling by boat and carriage for ten *li*, one arrives at Fuji.
Here lies the remains of the thousand-year-old poet Qu Yuan;
though his bones are cold, a subtle fragrance is perceived beneath the frosty leaves—a singular kind of loyalty and integrity within heaven and earth.
The vital energy suppresses the spring breeze, yet the myriad grasses flourish.
Answering the Venerable Dongzhou Fahua:
When weapons are turned upside down, one recognizes safety and peril; through skillful means and compassion, whom do you receive? Time and again, I see monks accompanying me face-to-face.
A laugh. The Gate of the Patriarchs is kept low;
the iron boat of Attendant Yuan has not yet consented to descend into the vast ocean. A message, without cause, has suddenly arrived: for six years on the Snowy Mountains, what was clarified?
Matter. I do not know whose eyes my own have been opened for.
Illness arises;
illness arises—how many jagged bone-stalks there are! With all my heart I lift them up, striving to sustain this life. I reflect upon the coarse hemp garments of my youth.
Matters. My path lies upon Mount Daxiong. Recalling my original aspiration in Qiantang, it has not ceased;
recalling Qiantang, I did not cross the river again for idle wandering. I regret that throughout my life I have been full of eccentricities.
Illness. At Mount Siming, Haolan opened his window and said to the Great Guest Master Zhaozhou, "Go drink tea.
Not even a single drop ever moistened his lips. Only upon reaching this point can one truly see him face-to-face.
It is attained. It does not hinder the full realization of both host and guest.
Two poems on remembering my mother:
her placenta was buried in a jar by the southern shore of the sea; the whale-waves now surround the earth and meet before my eyes. There is a precedent to follow, yet my heart is not yet at ease.
Stable. A rush-sandals cannot be sold for much coin.
The heavens are not high, nor the seas deep; where the white clouds fly, my heart is surely fixed. It is difficult for a rush-sandals to ascend the eyes of the age;
how much more so when the autumn wind turns the leaves golden?
Prefaces and Postscripts (Three Chapters):
Preface to the *Nanyou ji* (Collection from the Southern Tour).

Regarding famous mountains and sublime landscapes, those who have composed inscriptions and verses since antiquity are numerous. When poetry excels the landscape, the landscape is subsumed within the poetry; when the landscape excels...
If the poem does not enter into the realm, the poem and the realm remain separate; when the poem and the realm merge, seeing the poem is seeing the realm.
When the realm and the poem merge, seeing the realm is seeing the poem. Were it otherwise, both the poem and the realm would be lost.
The Zen master Zhizhi of Japan composed "Ten Odes on Tiantong," whose phrasing and meaning are extraordinary. I have recorded this to attest to its excellence.

Preface to the *Collection of Works from the Return to the East* The script is the same; the ruts of the chariots are the same; their physical forms are comparable, and their natures are similar. They study the language of Tang and discourse on the principles of the Way.

Though they are called people of Silla, they are originally the sons of the Śākya. These masters of the Zen school are my own kinsmen in the Dharma. Holding a scroll of verse, they have come to seek my words.
I have written this to bring it forth.
The *Baiyong Qinggui* and the *Chanyuan Qinggui* originated with Baizhang, who established rites and music to prevent human failings; through ritual, one establishes the Mean.
The Way uses joy to guide one’s nature and emotions. Incense, candles, tea, and soup serve as its rituals; bells, fish-shaped gongs, drums, and wooden clappers serve as its music.
When ritual and music do not falter, it is like a net having its main cord or a garment having its collar. By grasping the main cord and lifting the collar, one ensures there is no disorder.
The practice of this depends upon the master; without such a person, the main cord and net, or the collar and garment, will fall into chaos. [At] Mount Lu East...

The Reverend Master Xian of Linze compiled the monastic regulations and ritual protocols of former and contemporary venerable masters into ten volumes, titled *Cane-lin Bei-yong* (Essentials for the Chan Forest).
The detailed explanations of dignified deportment and minute conduct are exhaustive and exquisite; he intended to have them carved into printing blocks for wide circulation.

Alas, he has returned to stillness. At the time of his passing, he instructed his disciples to entrust the matter to the Librarian (Zangzhu) to exert all effort in completing these affairs, so as to rescue the collapsing legacy and serve as a model for a thousand ages.
Written respectfully on the day of the lifting of the retreat restrictions in the year Ding-si.
On the Succession of the Dharma in the Chan School (for the sake of Record-keeper Yu):

In the practice of Chan and the study of the Way, what is valued is the continuation of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' wisdom-life; it is not a matter for the glorification of one's own person. I have once said:
There are three ways of succeeding to this Dharma. The superior person succeeds to resentment; the middling person succeeds to gratitude; the inferior person succeeds to power.
He who succeeds to resentment abides in the Way; he who succeeds to gratitude abides in others; he who succeeds to power abides in himself.

Abiding in the Way is like pure gold in a great fire. Abiding in others is like the pine and cypress in the cold of winter. Abiding in oneself is like the willow in the spring breeze. Thus, one’s resolve is established.
The distinctions between the genuine and the spurious are not uniform; they have existed throughout the monastic communities of both ancient and modern times.

In composing this treatise, I am personally ashamed of my meager learning and inferior talent, and thus I dare not praise or condemn, nor judge the merits and faults of right and wrong. Hereafter, there will surely be those with the historian’s pen, such as Ban Gu or Yang Xiong, who will provide a detailed and supplementary account in the manner of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The Memorial of Various Mountains for the Installation of Master Dongming as Abbot of Baoying Chan Monastery on Mount Baiyun:
We humbly reflect that the Buddha appeared for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and the Patriarchs arose through the transmission of the Way. Fortunately, there are established precedents;
how could there not be those who come to study? We collectively honor the newly appointed Master Dongming of Baiyun, whose spirit is peerless and whose character rises loftily above the common crowd.
The deportment of Cui: In the chamber of the former Sage, he passed the meditation cushions and received the essential meaning face-to-face;
in the hall of Shuang'e, he borrowed a whisk and preached Zen with a loud voice. He exhausted the subtlety of the "Ying-axe" that carves the nose without error;

his merit surpasses Hou Yi’s archery that hits the eye of a sparrow—how could it be biased? A fine rain knows its season; white clouds appear amidst the black. All the mountains were eager to encourage his succession. One.
These words are certainly not mere rhetoric; I urge you to spur yourselves on and do not let your reins slacken.
Respectfully submitted. Lifting up the path of the advancing tiger cub at Shimen: outwardly no exterior is seen, inwardly no interior is seen.
Between heaven and earth, there is neither head nor tail. Those who face it are enlightened; those who turn their backs are in darkness. You all must directly speak forth its turning.
The phrase regarding the body was finally attained. [The Master] remarked: "The tiger cub takes a step, yet seeks the phrase for turning back from another.
*Yunwai Heshang Yulu* (Concluded).
My dharma-brother Cang formerly resided at Zhimen, where he devoted himself exclusively to this Way. After several years had passed, I heard...
The words of my late teacher have been collected and carved into printing blocks; there is a filial sentiment at work here.
Recently, he brought a volume past me and requested that I provide any missing or overlooked fragments to fulfill his purpose. Now that the carving is complete, I append this [note] at the end.
It was only fitting that it should be so. Written by the monk Wuyin, residing at Mount Xuedou.
The Biography of Chan Master Yungwai of Tiantong.
The master’s name was Yunxiu; his courtesy name was Yungwai, and his alternative style was Fangyan. His secular surname was Li, and his family had been natives of Changguo in Ming for generations.
From birth, he was small in stature, yet possessed a spirit that was vigorous and resolute. He served Master Zhigong of Zhiweng as his preceptor and received the tonsure.

He thoroughly investigated the fundamental tenets of the Caodong school until he reached their very source. Furthermore, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters throughout the monastic communities.

He first resided at Shimen in Cixi, then successively at Zhimen in Xiangshan and Tianning in Jun. Subsequently, urged by the three schools and the fourfold assembly, he succeeded to the seat of Zhuxi Tan and was elevated to the abbacy of Tiantong.
Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Within the red dust of the bustling marketplace, there is the bustling marketplace."
The Buddha-dharma is within the red dust; the Buddha-dharma is within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs.
Yesterday, when this mountain monk went out through the city gates, I momentarily forgot the Buddha-dharma amidst the clamor of the marketplace and the red dust.
Upon traveling twenty li to the Pines-and-Clouds [Village], I immediately beheld the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs. Great assembly, tell me: how is it so?
"This is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs. After a long silence, he said: "Pale white clouds drift lazily, appearing and disappearing amidst the vast void;
green creepers wind their way, climbing straight to the tops of cold pines. He then thanked the Head Seat, the Secretary, and the Librarian for presiding over the assembly.
He struck a circle with his whisk and said: "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
He struck another circle and said: "In ritual, harmony is prized; this is the beauty of the way of the former kings.
He struck another circle and said: "People do not recognize the mani jewel; it is personally found within the Tathāgatagarbha. "Do you all see it? he asked.

What they perceive differs, and each has its own strengths and weaknesses. Here at Tiandong, there is neither rigidity nor dogmatism. When the Master preaches the Dharma, he employs skillful metaphors and indirect guidance;
his aim is to stoop down to meet the student and bring them to completion through subtle means. Yet, when it comes to surging ahead and leaving all dust behind, he is unsurpassed.
Even those with the keen eyes of hawks or the pupils of dragons could find no way to peer into his presence. The transmission of this singular school of Dongshan relied solely upon him;
masters from the Three Han kingdoms and Japan alike turned toward him in admiration and longing. Those who came from all quarters to seek his instruction never had a day pass by without them.

Throughout his life, the Master was never haughty, never greedy for accumulation, and never took food for himself alone; whatever offerings he received, he distributed immediately to others, inspiring reverence in those who came after him.
He was increasingly meticulous in these matters, as he intended to serve as a patriarch of the school. At the two meal times, he would invariably carry his alms bowl himself to the hall.
Having passed away without any remaining assets, the practitioners pooled their funds to escort him to Tian Tong for burial. Liu Gongguan composed the inscription for his stupa.
His disciples who carried on his legacy were five: Dafang Pin, Dumu Sheng, Yuan’an Xing, Wuyin Zheng, and Dongling Yu.

Each was sufficient to expand their respective lineages. Dongling Yu alone entered Japan; the Japanese Emperor issued an edict for him to reside at the two great monasteries of Nanzen-ji and Tenryū-ji.
The Master once composed the *Baoming Sanmei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi); its profound meaning was widely transmitted throughout the monastic communities by Xing of Mount Jing.
Composed by the Bhikṣu Wénxiù of Wúxùn, Abbot of Shèngwànshòu Chán Monastery.

some are as small as the world, others as large as a coconut.

A Eulogy for Master Dongming, the Venerable Monk Dingxiang, which says:
His capacity is vast and profound; his deportment is extraordinary. His eyebrows part like clouds over the sea peaks; his eyes carry the moon of the Qín River. He has attained the ancient...
The fragrance of the cypress is transmitted; one enters the chamber of the realm of wondrous adornment. The profound mechanism borrows a path; the cavernous waters flow upstream.
The pervasive and the correct mutually merge; its merit remains unobscured. At times, a single phrase is spoken like striking a golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru;
at times, a single phrase is spoken like planting a jade tree before the crystal palace; at times, it is like a boat with oars of cassia and rudders of orchid.
The boat is free and at ease; sometimes it is like a surging mountain or a billowing house, crashing and surging. Its fame is as vast as the heavens, impossible to contain;
its earth-shaking wind and thunder are easily unleashed. This is what is called the orthodox transmission of the fifteenth generation of the Cao-Dong school.
Master Dongming was a master of Chan within the monastic community.
Preface to the *Dongming lu* (Record of Eastern Enlightenment).
The waters of Kunlun surge from the west and flow eastward; the waves of the vast blue sea rush and surge. The sun of Fusang rises in the east and returns to the west;
its light shines universally upon the heavens and earth of the land of India. The attendant Zhiji sat out the summer retreat in the mountains and presented this [text] to me.
The *Record of the Seven Assemblies of Master Dongming* and its recorded dialogues and opportunities for instruction are radiant and brilliant, like the great function of the moon reflected in water.
From this, the various branches and lineages of the Dongshan school flourished. The epitaph states: "To the east is Dongming;
to the west is Ximing. Since the Way has no fixed location, it is called 'Great Illumination' (Daming). These words are exhaustive.
I have nothing further with which to embellish it.

The *Epilogue to the Chanlin Songgu Ji* and the *Lianzhu Songgu Tongji* take the original and make it even more beautiful; their phrasing becomes intricate and their expressions thorny, emerging more and more in ever-increasing abundance. As it is said:
Bees brew honey from a hundred flowers; ants weave silk through nine-folded pearls. Those who eat the honey think of the bees;
those who cherish the pearls long for the ants. I have made this statement, when a guest stepped forward and said:
"Suppose we suddenly encounter one who does not eat honey, who does not prize pearls, and who has no taste for words or writing—what would become of this collection? I replied: "It is a sickness."
The patient could not fall ill of his own accord; the visitor felt ashamed and withdrew. Thus was this written. "Spring of the Zhizhi era:
Clouds from Tiantong Mountain," inscribed by Xu.
One day, the Master asked Wuyin, "Tiantong has died a great death today; how will you save him?"
Yin said, "I invite the Master to eat. The Master said, "Today, Tiantong has died a great death;
you must not try to save him. Yin asked, "Why would I save him? The Master spoke again, "Today, Tiantong has died a great death;
who will walk with me? Yin replied, "The Master goes first; I shall follow behind. The Master laughed heartily.

From this point on, the relationship between master and disciple was precise to the finest detail, like that between Master Guishan and his son Jue. (From the *Record of Master Yongjue of Gushan*, continuing the lineage lamp.
A memorial from various mountains for the Reverend Yungwai’s second tenure at Tiantong, written by Chan Master Xiaoyin Yin of Longxiang.

When Dayang transmitted the Dharma and established the orphaned lineage, it was as difficult as the ordeal of Ying and Jiu; when Biancai emerged from the mountains, those who returned were like the multitudes of Qi and Bin.
One truly knows that it depends on virtue and not on force. Who does not have both ancestors and descendants? Yet here we are, so insignificant.
How could this be tolerated? His spirit is nurtured in profound serenity, and his speech emerges with natural perfection. Within his breast, he has cleared away all boundaries and distinctions;
his lofty character stirs the greed and timidity of others. Like the vast sky, a single expanse of azure, it is like the brilliant dawn-star of the east; surrounded by all the peaks, it stands alone.
The Great White Mountain of the majestic snow peaks has long been protected by divine dragons; it does not bend like a silkworm seeking to stretch its body.
Though the paths of the world branch into many directions—whether south or north—the official records provide mutual relief. May our relations be as firm as jade and as precious as gold;
let us renew our solemn alliance to further deepen our ancient friendship.
When Master Yunwai resided at Tiantong, the various mountain monasteries issued this memorial:
"In Yan-nan, the official Sa Tianxi is like the long-tailed star Chang-geng (Venus) paired with the waning moon.

The Great Dharma of the South: since you have already departed without a fixed mind, what can even those who possess power do?
I am an *udumbara* flower in this world, a lion among the Śākyas. At Shimen, vast and far-reaching, the birds of the sky do not encounter people;

in the depths of the blue sea, who has seen the lotus first emerging from the water? Moreover, having already entered the marketplace to extend a helping hand, it does not hinder one from recognizing the illusion.
The ancient cypress lies across the waves, rising from Xi-zhou in safety; the extraordinary sprouts flourish luxuriantly, as the Marquis Yang Guang is exceptionally numinous.
May they strengthen my jaw and cheek, and assist your banners and drums.
Lamenting for the Elder Yunwai, Venerable Dongming Huirui:

The waters and sky are vast and empty; at last, distance is forgotten. The Great White Peak towers high, gazing toward the Nine Heavens. His countenance remains solemn beyond clouds and rain. Who would say that life and death do not share the same root?
(On the twenty-second day of the eighth month of the Jiazi year of the Taiding era, he passed away with serene composure. His secular age was eighty-three, and his monastic seniority was sixty-five.)

For over twenty years, I have wandered like a drifting weed among the rivers and lakes. I have gained a rough understanding that the various lineages originate from a single source and possess no differing flavors.

I have enjoyed reading the works of various masters; while the writings on Linji are so numerous they fill the rafters and drive oxen from their stalls, I often lament that the teachings of the Dongshan lineage have rarely circulated within the monastic forests.
It is imperative that the noble words and exemplary conduct of the former worthies not remain unrecorded.

Furthermore, to disdainfully cast aside the traces of words and texts as impediments to the illumination of the Way—leaving them to rot in the bellies of bookworms or fall into the hands of children—is this not an extreme form of stinginess toward the world?
Consequently, the precious chariot of the guide has been damaged, and the path home is lost;
it is no small matter that even these sublime words and noble deeds have been obscured. The Venerable Gufan cherished the virtues of the former masters...

These subtle words—this record you once graciously bestowed upon me—I have read. As I examined his words for proclaiming the school, he directly reveals the truth rather than resorting to circuitous explanations;
he does not rigidly adhere to the "Cavern" (Dong) alone, yet his integration of the partial and the perfect naturally accords with that Cavern. It is like the movement of vast clouds:

whether emerging or vanishing, manifesting or concealing, they act with sovereign ease. As I spread it out and read it at this time, the defilements of my mind and eyes are cleansed, and I am filled with joy beyond measure.

It is excellent. There have been several instances of treasuring and transmitting this work, carving it onto bamboo slips and copying it onto wooden blocks for posterity. Last year, due to certain circumstances, I took up residence in the capital for six seasons, passing through both winter and summer.
My meals were of thin rice gruel, and my firewood was of "jade" (fine wood) and "cinnamon" (precious incense).

With no surplus coins remaining in my purse, I harbored a long-held desire to lodge [this text] in a thatched hut, entrusting it to the young novice monk Zhuangfeng Zongjian. Moved by his profound reputation and inspired by his devotion, he joyfully donated his pure wealth.

The courageous resolve of [Master] Yongwei is truly commendable. Thus, I have searched through lost and scattered fragments and managed to recover only a few pieces, which I have appended to the end of this volume.
However, regarding such matters as his initial residence at Shimen and his subsequent relocation from Tianning to Tiantong, these accounts have vanished beyond recovery;
one can do nothing but harbor deep sighs of regret. As for the master’s life history and travels, they are recorded in the *Nanshi Shuzhong Zhuan*.
The *Biography and Eulogy of Master Xiangyin* already provides a rough account of this.
Song Lian of Jinhua also praised the Master’s fame and virtue as being equal to those of the two masters Xugou and Huiji. Liu Gongguan, the Hanlin Waitzhi, inscribed his stupa stone, saying:
"It is only fitting that the ancient Buddha Hongzhi has appeared once more in the world. During the era of the Yuan dynasty, the Master was a prominent descendant of the Dong lineage.

He was like a solitary star in the sky; the masses vied with one another to behold him. The three kingdoms of Korea and Japan looked toward his influence with longing and admiration, attending his rites without a single day’s interval.

Generally speaking, since our own country entered the Yuan dynasty, many eminent monks have appeared in the annals of the Sangha who received his exhortations and encouragement upon visiting him in audience.
Yet, as for those whose spiritual resonance was like the meeting of a needle and its eye, such individuals were nearly non-existent.

I, Yong, reflect back on the past when the style of our teacher’s school was steep and profound. The subtlety of his forging and the skill of his refining were such that he was acclaimed as authoritative by all quarters.
Even those with the "tiger-head" [of talent] who held their own horns entered his gate;
they were like Qin Wuyang, who, carrying the map of Yan, went to the court of Qin and sought refuge with Yi Shui, yet could not return, trembling in fear before the palace steps.
"Is this not like constructing the innermost sanctum? It was barely enough to provide the funds for five people to receive ordination.
Alas, though it has passed through three generations of transmission, we have yet to hear of anyone who has inherited the lineage up to the present day. I, Yong, fortunately obtained this record;

the woodblocks have already been carved, and I have thus noted this rare encounter at the end of the scroll. When the brothers of the monastic community asked with surprise about the origin of this, I rose from my seat and said: 'I..."
I am unable to know [the answer]. I request that you consult Master Fan (Fan Shangren) on this matter.
